title: A list built with room for ten
scenario: The seating chart pre-sizes an ArrayList for ten seats and then assigns seat 0. It crashes before printing anything.
symptom:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.IndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 0 out of bounds for length 0
	at java.base/jdk.internal.util.Preconditions.outOfBounds(Preconditions.java:100)
	at java.base/jdk.internal.util.Preconditions.outOfBoundsCheckIndex(Preconditions.java:106)
	at java.base/jdk.internal.util.Preconditions.checkIndex(Preconditions.java:302)
	at java.base/java.util.Objects.checkIndex(Objects.java:385)
	at java.base/java.util.ArrayList.set(ArrayList.java:470)
	at Main.main(Main.java:6)
question: What's the root cause?
options: 10 is capacity, not size; the list is empty so set(0) is out of range
ArrayList(10) creates an immutable list that rejects set()
set() needs a LinkedList; ArrayList only supports add()
The capacity must be a power of two, so 10 is rejected
explanation: The int argument to new ArrayList<>(10) is the initial capacity of the backing array, not the number of elements. A fresh list always has size() == 0 regardless of capacity. List.set(index, e) replaces an existing element and requires 0 <= index < size(), so set(0) on an empty list throws IndexOutOfBoundsException. Use add() to grow a list, or Collections.nCopies / Arrays.asList when you really want pre-filled slots.
fixNote: Used seats.add("Ana") instead of set(0, ...), since the list starts empty.
debugTip: Set a breakpoint on line 6 and evaluate seats.size(); it is 0, so no index is valid for set().

title: The VIP jumps the queue and someone vanishes
scenario: A VIP should be inserted at position 1 of the waiting list, pushing everyone else back. Instead the list stays the same length and Bo is gone.
question: What's the root cause?
options: List.of made the copy immutable, so the insert was partly ignored
set(1, x) overwrites the element at 1; add(1, x) inserts and shifts
Indexes start at 1 in List, so set(1) replaced the first person
set() appends to the end and then removes the duplicate entry
explanation: List.set(index, e) replaces the element at that position and returns the old one; the size never changes. List.add(index, e) inserts at that position and shifts the current element and everything after it one place to the right, growing the list by one. Because set was used, Bo was overwritten by VIP. The copy into new ArrayList<>(...) is fully mutable, so immutability is not the problem.
fixNote: Replaced q.set(1, "VIP") with q.add(1, "VIP") to insert instead of overwrite.
debugTip: Step over line 7 with a watch on q and q.size(); the size staying at 3 shows an overwrite, not an insert.

title: Staff grouped by team, sorted by name
scenario: The roster should be grouped by team (A before B) and alphabetical within each team. It comes out purely alphabetical with teams mixed.
symptom:
Prints:
B Amy
B Bob
A Kim
A Zed
question: Which fix is correct?
options: Use Collections.sort instead, because List.sort is not stable
Sort by team twice so the grouping survives the name sort
Sort by name first, then by team; the stable second sort keeps names
Replace both sorts with a single sort on name, then reverse()
explanation: List.sort and Collections.sort are both guaranteed stable: elements that compare equal keep their existing relative order. With two passes, the LAST sort becomes the primary key and the earlier sort only decides ties. Sorting by team last means the team grouping wins and the earlier name order survives inside each team. A single comparator, comparing(P::team).thenComparing(P::name), says the same thing more directly.
fixNote: Swapped the two sorts so team (the primary key) is sorted last.
debugTip: Put a breakpoint after line 9 and after line 10 and inspect ps each time; the second sort scrambles the grouping the first one built.
buggyOutput:
B Amy
B Bob
A Kim
A Zed
fixedOutput:
A Kim
A Zed
B Amy
B Bob

title: Oldest first, ties alphabetical
scenario: Players should be listed by age, oldest first, and players of the same age alphabetically. The ties come out in reverse alphabetical order.
question: What's the root cause?
options: thenComparing only runs when ages differ, so names are never compared
comparingInt boxes the ages, so equal ages compare as different objects
List.sort is unstable, so ties end up in an arbitrary order
reversed() at the end reverses the whole chain, including the name tie-break
explanation: Each Comparator method returns a new comparator wrapping everything built so far. Calling reversed() last wraps the entire age-then-name comparator, so both keys are flipped: ages descend, but names descend too. To reverse only the age, call reversed() straight after comparingInt(U::age) and then add thenComparing(U::name). Alternatively write comparing(U::age, Comparator.reverseOrder()) so the reversal is scoped to that key.
fixNote: Moved reversed() to apply only to the age comparator, before thenComparing(U::name).
debugTip: Evaluate the comparator on two same-age users (Ann, Bea) in the debugger; a positive result shows names are being compared in reverse.

title: What does put hand back?
scenario: A developer logs the result of each put call on a price map, assuming it echoes the value just stored.
question: What does this print?
options:
null
3
5

null
null
5
explanation: Map.put returns the PREVIOUS value associated with the key, or null if there was none. The first put has nothing to replace, so it returns null; the second replaces 3 and returns 3. The map then holds 5. This return value is handy for detecting overwrites, but a null result is ambiguous if the map can store null values, in which case use containsKey.
fixNote: Captured put's return value as the old value and labelled it explicitly.
debugTip: Use evaluate expression on price.put(...) at a breakpoint before line 6 to see what is returned, then inspect the map entry.

title: Every word appears exactly once?
scenario: The word counter should report how many times each word appears. Every count comes out as 1, even for repeated words.
question: What's the root cause?
options: merge only inserts absent keys and ignores keys already present
The remapping function returns the new value 1 instead of old + 1
TreeMap.merge resets values to the default when keys are equal
split(" ") yields distinct String objects, so keys never match
explanation: Map.merge(key, value, fn) stores value if the key is absent; if it is present, it stores fn.apply(oldValue, value), and if fn returns null the entry is removed. Here fn returns its second argument, the fresh 1, so every repeat just overwrites the count with 1. Integer::sum combines old and new, giving a proper counter. Keys match fine because maps compare with equals/compareTo, not identity.
fixNote: Used Integer::sum as the remapping function so repeats add to the count.
debugTip: Set a breakpoint inside the lambda on line 8 and watch old and one; you will see old grow nowhere because the lambda discards it.

title: Grouping orders by customer
scenario: Orders should be collected into a list per customer. The program crashes on the very first order.
symptom:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "java.util.List.add(Object)" because the return value of "java.util.Map.putIfAbsent(Object, Object)" is null
	at Main.main(Main.java:10)
question: What's the root cause?
options: TreeMap rejects ArrayList values because lists are not Comparable
The new ArrayList is garbage-collected before add() runs
putIfAbsent returns the previous value, which is null on first insert
putIfAbsent throws when the key is absent, by design
explanation: putIfAbsent(k, v) returns the value that was already mapped, or null if it just inserted v. On the first order for a customer it inserts the list but returns null, so .add(i) is called on null. computeIfAbsent(k, fn) instead returns the current (existing or newly computed) value, which is exactly what you want to chain on. It also only creates the list when needed rather than allocating one on every call.
fixNote: Switched to computeIfAbsent(cs[i], k -> new ArrayList<>()), which returns the list in the map.
debugTip: Add an exception breakpoint on NullPointerException; at line 9, evaluate the putIfAbsent result to see it is null.

title: Undo restores the oldest edit
scenario: An undo stack should pop the most recent edit first. Undo returns the very first edit instead.
symptom:
Prints:
undo: type A
undo: type B
question: Which fix is correct?
options: Use poll() instead of pop(), since pop() reads from the tail
Replace ArrayDeque with a PriorityQueue to keep newest first
Call undo.reversed() before popping to flip the order
Use push() to add, so additions and pop() both work on the head
explanation: A Deque has two ends. offer/add/addLast put elements at the tail (queue style), while push/addFirst put them at the head (stack style). pop() and poll() both remove from the head. Mixing offer with pop therefore gives FIFO behaviour: the oldest edit comes out first. Use push with pop (LIFO stack) or offer with poll (FIFO queue), never a mix.
fixNote: Replaced offer() with push() so new edits go on the head where pop() takes them.
debugTip: Watch undo after each offer on lines 6-8; the debugger's element order shows the newest edit at the tail, away from where pop() reads.
buggyOutput:
undo: type A
undo: type B

title: Shipping band for a 7 kg parcel
scenario: Bands start at 0, 5 and 10 kg; a parcel uses the band whose start is at or below its weight. A 7 kg parcel is charged the 10 kg rate.
question: What's the root cause?
options: ceilingKey returns the smallest key >= 7; floorKey gives the largest <= 7
ceilingKey rounds 7 up to the nearest multiple of five
TreeMap keeps keys in insertion order, so 10 is found first
get(band) falls back to the last entry when the key is missing
explanation: TreeMap's navigation methods find neighbouring keys: floorKey(k) is the greatest key <= k, ceilingKey(k) the least key >= k, and lowerKey/higherKey are the strict < and > versions. A band lookup 'start at or below the weight' is a floor query, which gives 5. ceilingKey(7) returns 10, the next band up. All four return null when no such key exists, so unboxing into an int can also throw NPE for out-of-range inputs.
fixNote: Used floorKey(kg) instead of ceilingKey(kg).
debugTip: At a breakpoint on line 10, evaluate fee.floorKey(kg) and fee.ceilingKey(kg) side by side to see which neighbour each picks.

title: How many scores are 80 or below?
scenario: The report should count students scoring 80 or less. The student who scored exactly 80 is left out.
question: Which fix is correct?
options: Call tailMap(80) because headMap returns keys above the bound
Call headMap(80, true); one-argument headMap excludes the key 80
Call headMap(81); headMap(80) skips keys equal to 79 and 80
Call subMap(0, 80) because headMap only covers the first key
explanation: SortedMap.headMap(toKey) returns the keys strictly less than toKey: the upper bound is exclusive, matching the half-open convention of subMap(from, to) and String.substring. NavigableMap adds headMap(toKey, inclusive) so you can include the bound explicitly. tailMap(fromKey) is the opposite: inclusive of fromKey by default. The returned map is a live view, so later puts into s show up in it too.
fixNote: Used headMap(80, true) to make the upper bound inclusive.
debugTip: At a breakpoint on line 11, evaluate s.headMap(80) and s.headMap(80, true) and compare the keys they contain.

title: The cache evicts the page just viewed
scenario: A 2-entry LRU cache should evict the least recently USED page. After reading 'home' again and adding 'cart', 'home' is evicted anyway.
question: What's the root cause?
options: removeEldestEntry runs before the put, so it removes the wrong entry
LinkedHashMap ignores get() calls made on anonymous subclasses
accessOrder is false, so get() doesn't move 'home'; order stays insertion
The load factor 0.75 forces a rehash that reorders entries randomly
explanation: LinkedHashMap keeps a linked list of entries in insertion order by default. The third constructor argument, accessOrder, switches it to access order: every get or put of an existing key moves that entry to the end. removeEldestEntry is consulted after each put and removes the head of that list. With accessOrder false, 'home' remains the eldest despite being read, so it is evicted; with true, 'shop' becomes eldest.
fixNote: Passed true as the accessOrder argument of the LinkedHashMap constructor.
debugTip: Watch lru.keySet() after the get on line 14; if 'home' doesn't move to the end, the map is not in access order.

title: Pairing up names from a list
scenario: The loop should print each name next to its length. It prints some garbled pairs and then crashes.
symptom:
Exception in thread "main" java.util.NoSuchElementException
	at java.base/java.util.ImmutableCollections$ListItr.next(ImmutableCollections.java:382)
	at Main.main(Main.java:9)
question: What's the root cause?
options: List.of iterators are single-use and throw on the second hasNext
length() is evaluated before next(), so it reads a null element
hasNext() advances the iterator, so the loop skips one element
next() is called twice per iteration, skipping ahead past the end
explanation: Every call to Iterator.next() returns the next element AND advances the cursor. Calling it twice in one loop body consumes two elements per check of hasNext(), pairing Ann with Bobby's length. With an odd number of elements, the second next() runs when nothing is left and throws NoSuchElementException. Call next() once, store the result in a variable, and use the variable.
fixNote: Stored it.next() in a local variable and used it twice.
debugTip: Set a breakpoint on line 8 and step into each next() call; watching the iterator's cursor shows it advancing twice per pass.

title: Duplicate ticket detector flags everyone
scenario: The scanner should flag a ticket only when it has already been seen. It flags every ticket except the repeated one.
question: What's the root cause?
options: add() returns true when the element was NEW; the condition is inverted
add() returns the set's new size, which is always truthy here
Autoboxed Integers above 127 never compare equal in a HashSet
HashSet.add throws on duplicates, and the exception is swallowed
explanation: Set.add(e) returns true if the set changed, meaning e was not already present, and false if it was a duplicate. That makes add a one-step 'check and insert', but the duplicate case is the false branch. Here the condition fires on every first sighting and stays silent for the real duplicate. Boxed Integer keys are compared with equals and hashCode in a HashSet, so the 127 cache is irrelevant.
fixNote: Negated the condition: if (!seen.add(t)) reports duplicates.
debugTip: Set a breakpoint on line 8 and evaluate seen.add(t) mentally per ticket; note it is false exactly once, for the second 101.

title: The longest word is 'pear'?
scenario: The app should show the longest word in the list and how often it appears. It reports 'pear' instead of 'banana'.
question: Which fix is correct?
options: Use Collections.min, since max returns the shortest string
Pass Comparator.comparingInt(String::length) to Collections.max
Sort the list first; max only works on sorted collections
Replace frequency with a loop, because frequency changes the order
explanation: Collections.max(coll) uses the elements' natural ordering, which for String is lexicographic (dictionary) order, so 'pear' beats 'kiwi' and 'banana'. To compare by another property, use the overload Collections.max(coll, comparator). Collections.frequency(coll, o) counts elements equal to o using equals, and works on any collection without sorting. Neither method modifies the list.
fixNote: Passed a length comparator to Collections.max.
debugTip: Evaluate "pear".compareTo("banana") at a breakpoint on line 7; a positive result shows max is using alphabetical order.

title: A config map that never loads
scenario: A small settings map is built with Map.of. The program dies on startup before printing anything.
symptom:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: duplicate key: host
	at java.base/java.util.ImmutableCollections$MapN.<init>(ImmutableCollections.java:1196)
	at java.base/java.util.Map.of(Map.java:1407)
	at Main.main(Main.java:5)
question: What's the root cause?
options: Map.of allows at most two entries; the third one overflows
Map.of values must differ, and "db1" equals "db2" by hash
Map.of rejects duplicate keys instead of keeping the last value
Map.of requires the keys to be passed in sorted order
explanation: The Map.of and Map.ofEntries factories build immutable maps and throw IllegalArgumentException if any key appears twice, unlike HashMap.put which silently overwrites. They also reject null keys and values with NullPointerException. Set.of likewise rejects duplicate elements. This fail-fast design catches copy-paste mistakes in literal maps at construction time.
fixNote: Removed the duplicate "host" key, keeping the intended value.
debugTip: Add an exception breakpoint on IllegalArgumentException; the message names the duplicate key so you can search the literal for it.

title: Checking a list for a missing value
scenario: A validator checks whether a list of allowed roles contains the user's role, which may be null. It crashes for anonymous users.
symptom:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException
	at java.base/java.util.Objects.requireNonNull(Objects.java:233)
	at java.base/java.util.ImmutableCollections$List12.indexOf(ImmutableCollections.java:597)
	at java.base/java.util.ImmutableCollections$AbstractImmutableList.contains(ImmutableCollections.java:331)
	at Main.main(Main.java:7)
question: What's the root cause?
options: contains() unboxes the String and fails on the null reference
An immutable list throws on every query, not just on writes
contains() calls role.equals(...), which ArrayList would avoid
List.of lists are null-hostile: even contains(null) throws NPE
explanation: The immutable collections from List.of, Set.of and Map.of do not allow null elements, and their query methods are null-hostile too: contains(null) and indexOf(null) throw NullPointerException rather than returning false. An ArrayList would simply return false. Guard the lookup with a null check, or copy into a null-tolerant collection if nulls are legitimately expected.
fixNote: Added a role != null check before calling contains.
debugTip: Add an exception breakpoint on NullPointerException; the top frames are inside ImmutableCollections, showing the list itself rejected null.

title: Three tasks capture a counter
scenario: To get around the effectively-final rule, the code captures a one-element array as a counter. Each task is meant to print the number it was created with.
question: What does this print?
explanation: A lambda can only capture local variables that are effectively final, and it captures their VALUE at creation. Here the captured variable is the array reference n, which never changes, so it compiles, but all three lambdas share the same array and read n[0] only when they run. By then the loop has left n[0] at 2. Declaring a fresh effectively final local inside the loop (int k = i) gives each lambda its own snapshot.
fixNote: Captured a per-iteration local int k = i instead of a shared array slot.
debugTip: Set a breakpoint inside the lambda on line 9 and inspect n when it runs; all three tasks see the same array object.

title: Lowercase names sorted after Zoe
scenario: The contact list should be alphabetical ignoring case. 'adam' and 'bea' appear after 'Zoe'.
question: What's the root cause?
options: The method reference binds to the first element, not each pair
compareTo compares UTF-16 codes, where all uppercase precede lowercase
List.sort ignores the comparator for String and uses hash order
compareTo compares lengths first, then letters
explanation: String::compareTo is an unbound instance method reference, so it acts as a Comparator<String> where (a, b) -> a.compareTo(b). compareTo compares char values, and 'A'..'Z' (65-90) all come before 'a'..'z' (97-122), so every capitalised name sorts first. String::compareToIgnoreCase, or the ready-made String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER, folds case before comparing. For human-language sorting with accents, use a java.text.Collator.
fixNote: Sorted with String::compareToIgnoreCase.
debugTip: Evaluate "Zoe".compareTo("adam") at a breakpoint on line 7; it is negative, proving uppercase wins.

title: Add tax, then a fee, or the other way?
scenario: A price pipeline composes two functions: add a $10 fee and double the price. The author expected 'fee first' from compose.
question: What does this print?
explanation: f.andThen(g) returns x -> g(f(x)): f runs first, then g. f.compose(g) returns x -> f(g(x)): the ARGUMENT g runs first. So fee.compose(dbl) doubles 5 to 10 and then adds the fee for 20, while fee.andThen(dbl) adds the fee to get 15 and doubles to 30. Read andThen left to right; read compose like mathematical composition, right to left.
fixNote: Used dbl.compose(fee) so both lines apply the fee first and print 30.
debugTip: Put breakpoints inside both lambdas on lines 5 and 6 and run line 7; the order in which they hit shows which function runs first.

title: Counting words across sentences
scenario: The stream should count every word across three sentences (7 words). It prints 3.
question: Which fix is correct?
options: Use map(s -> s.split(" ").length) and keep count()
Call distinct() before count() so arrays are expanded
Replace count() with collect(Collectors.counting())
Use flatMap(s -> Arrays.stream(s.split(" "))) to flatten words
explanation: map is one-to-one: each sentence becomes exactly one String[], so the stream still has three elements and count() returns 3. flatMap is one-to-many: the function returns a Stream for each element, and those streams are concatenated into one flat stream of words. Arrays.stream(array) or Stream.of(array) turns each split result into such a stream. Collectors.counting() would count the same three arrays.
fixNote: Replaced map with flatMap(s -> Arrays.stream(s.split(" "))).
debugTip: Insert .peek(System.out::println) after line 9; it prints three array references like [Ljava.lang.String;@..., not words.

title: The product of 1 to 5 is zero
scenario: The stream multiplies the numbers 1 to 5 and should print 120. It prints 0.
question: What's the root cause?
options: The identity must be 1 for multiplication; 0 * anything stays 0
reduce skips the first element when an identity is given
Integer overflow during boxing turns the product into zero
The lambda's parameters are swapped, so it divides instead
explanation: reduce(identity, op) starts the accumulation from identity and folds each element in with op. The identity must be a neutral element for op, meaning op(identity, x) == x: 0 for addition, 1 for multiplication, "" for concatenation. Starting from 0 makes every product 0. A wrong identity is also counted once per chunk in parallel streams, so it gives inconsistent results there too.
fixNote: Changed the identity from 0 to 1.
debugTip: Set a breakpoint inside the lambda on line 7 and watch a; it is 0 on the first call and never changes.

title: Adding a bonus item to the results
scenario: After filtering cheap items into a list, the code appends one bonus item. It crashes on the append.
symptom:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException
	at java.base/java.util.ImmutableCollections.uoe(ImmutableCollections.java:142)
	at java.base/java.util.ImmutableCollections$AbstractImmutableCollection.add(ImmutableCollections.java:147)
	at Main.main(Main.java:9)
question: What's the root cause?
options: filter() made the stream read-only, so any later list is too
Stream.toList() returns an unmodifiable list, so add() is refused
The source List.of is immutable and toList() is a live view of it
toList() returns a fixed-size array-backed list like Arrays.asList
explanation: Stream.toList() (Java 16+) returns an unmodifiable List, so add, remove and set throw UnsupportedOperationException. Collectors.toList() currently returns an ArrayList, but its contract promises nothing about mutability, so you should not rely on that either. When you need to modify the result, ask for it explicitly with Collectors.toCollection(ArrayList::new) or copy with new ArrayList<>(...). The result is a new list, not a view of the source.
fixNote: Collected into an explicit ArrayList with Collectors.toCollection(ArrayList::new).
debugTip: Evaluate cheap.getClass() at a breakpoint on line 9; it is an ImmutableCollections list, not ArrayList.

title: Tag list with brackets in odd places
scenario: Tags should print as [java, sql, git]. Instead the brackets appear between tags and the commas are on the outside.
question: Which fix is correct?
options: Use joining(", ") and add brackets with String.format inside map
Use reduce("[", String::concat) followed by + "]"
Pass arguments as (delimiter, prefix, suffix): joining(", ", "[", "]")
Swap the stream for String.join, which accepts a prefix first
explanation: Collectors.joining(delimiter, prefix, suffix) takes the delimiter FIRST, then the prefix and suffix that wrap the whole result. Passing "[" first makes it the separator between elements while ", " wraps the outside. The prefix and suffix are added even for an empty stream, giving "[]". String.join(delim, items) only supports a delimiter.
fixNote: Reordered the arguments to joining(", ", "[", "]").
debugTip: Use evaluate expression on the joining call at line 8 and hover the parameter names in the IDE; the first is 'delimiter'.

title: Page 2 of the results is empty
scenario: With 3 items per page, page 2 should show items 4 to 6. It prints an empty list.
question: What's the root cause?
options: skip counts from 1, so skip(3) jumps past the end of the range
rangeClosed(1, 8) yields 8 empty pages until boxed() runs
boxed() turns the stream unordered, so skip drops random items
limit runs first, keeping only 3 items, then skip(3) discards all
explanation: Stream operations apply in the order they are written, each to the output of the previous one. limit(3) keeps 1, 2, 3, and skip(3) then discards those three, leaving nothing. For pagination, skip the earlier pages first and then limit to the page size. On ordered streams both operations respect encounter order.
fixNote: Moved skip(...) before limit(size).
debugTip: Insert .peek(x -> System.out.println("after limit " + x)) between lines 9 and 10 to see what reaches skip.

title: Summing 1 to 10 gives 45
scenario: The stream should add the numbers from 1 to 10 inclusive (55). It prints 45.
question: What's the root cause?
options: range(a, b) excludes b; rangeClosed(a, b) includes it
range starts from 0 regardless of the first argument
sum() drops the largest element to avoid overflow
range(1, 10) steps by 2 when the bounds are both even
explanation: IntStream.range(start, end) is half-open: it yields start up to end - 1, like a for loop with i < end. IntStream.rangeClosed(start, end) includes end. So range(1, 10) is 1..9, summing to 45. The same half-open convention appears in List.subList, String.substring and TreeMap.headMap.
fixNote: Used IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 10).
debugTip: Evaluate IntStream.range(1, 10).max() at a breakpoint on line 5; it reports 9, not 10.
